I reviewed Alienware’s shockingly affordable $350 AW2726DM earlier this week , and that 1440p OLED actually hits a much faster 240Hz. The AW3226Q is special because it’s the first OLED I’ve used that feels truly uncompromised as an everyday PC monitor . I’m a writer. I spend most of my working life staring at Word documents, web browsers, spreadsheets, Slack, and all the other decidedly booooring things people actually do with their computers. Traditional OLED gaming monitors have always come with an asterisk for that sort of work: Their unusual subpixel layouts can create visible color fringing around text. Then, when the workday ends, I’m an intensely competitive gamer who regularly slays noobs at 240Hz and beyond. Those two sides of my PC life have traditionally wanted different monitors. I’m a filthy monitor pervert who actually swaps out several different models depending on what I’m working on or playing. But the 32-inch, 4K Alienware AW3226Q finally makes me want the same display for both. At $699, that’s a hell of an accomplishment. RGB stripe is the real breakthrough When Alienware announced the AW3226Q , I immediately zeroed in on its new RGB-stripe Tandem OLED panel. I had already seen LG Display’s new RGB-stripe technology at CES , and while improved OLED brightness and other technical advancements are always welcome, this seemingly boring change was the one that really grabbed my attention. Why? Text. Most OLED gaming monitors don’t use the conventional red, green, and blue subpixel arrangement that Windows expects, which can result in colored fringes around fine text. Higher pixel densities help mask the effect, and some people are more sensitive to it than others. But once you notice it, it’s hard to stop noticing it. I notice it. OLED text fringing example from the Corsair Xeneon Flex. I certainly noticed it on Alienware’s $350 AW2726DM earlier this week. That monitor is an absolutely killer value for gaming, but between its dimmer panel and visible text fringing, I wouldn’t want to use it as my primary work display. The new Alienware AW3226Q is different, and you can see its difference in the screenshots above — the left image is Alienware’s new display, while the right image shows text fringing on the otherwise excellent Corsair Xeneon Flex from a couple years back. The Alienware’s traditional RGB stripe makes text look crisp and clean in a way I’m simply not accustomed to seeing from an OLED gaming monitor. Text fringing is all but eliminated. I’ve spent hours working on the AW3226Q, and Word documents and web pages just look right . That matters more to me than another hundred hertz ever could. OLED monitors have already conquered gaming. Their perfect blacks, luscious colors, and virtually instantaneous pixel response make them phenomenal for it. Making it just as good for the boring stuff you do between sessions? That’s been the real challenge. Alienware finally cracked it. And the image quality is glorious Brad Chacos/Foundry Don’t let all this talk about Microsoft Word give you the wrong impression. The AW3226Q absolutely rips when it’s time to play. It’s jaw-dropping in action. The glossy 4K Tandem OLED panel is bright, vibrant, and bursting with contrast. Colors leap off the screen against OLED’s wonderfully deep blacks. Games look sharp at 4K across the 32-inch display, and everything has the sort of visual punch that makes going back to a conventional LCD difficult. Playing around with Alan Wake 2 on this do-it-all beast is simply magnificent . It’s especially striking after spending time with Alienware’s $350 OLED. I love what Alienware accomplished there, but you can see some of the compromises required to hit that price. Its panel runs darker than I’d like, while the AW3226Q is playing in another league. Everything just has more punch here. And 4K across 32 inches is a fantastic match. Games look razor-sharp, while the large, high-resolution screen provides plenty of room to spread out when you’re actually getting things done. The AW3226Q isn’t merely a great gaming display that I can tolerate for work. It’s excellent at both. Finally . About that 165Hz refresh rate There’s one obvious objection to calling the Alienware AW3226Q a no-compromises monitor: Its refresh rate tops out at 165Hz. That’s substantially slower than the 240Hz OLED I reviewed earlier this week, never mind the 360Hz, 480Hz, and even faster displays available to esports diehards these days. And I can tell the difference. I’ve become accustomed to 240Hz-and-faster monitors for competitive gaming. Dropping back to 165Hz isn’t some imperceptible distinction that exists only on a spec sheet. If you’re the sort of person who tunes every graphics setting for maximum frames and minimum latency, there are better monitors for that specific job. For everybody else, 165Hz is fantastic. OLED’s lightning-fast pixel response keeps motion crisp, and 165Hz is plenty fast enough to make everything from shooters to sprawling single-player adventures feel wonderfully smooth and responsive. It’s also worth remembering what we’re talking about driving here: 4K games at up to 165 frames per second. Even today’s monstrous graphics cards can have their hands full trying to do that in cutting-edge games. Would I prefer this exact monitor at 240Hz? Of course. Would I pay substantially more or sacrifice the things that make the AW3226Q so good everywhere else to get it? Nope. A compromise can exist on a spec sheet without meaningfully compromising the experience. Alienware nailed the balance here. Alienware compromised in the right places You can see the same philosophy elsewhere. The AW3226Q doesn’t have built-in speakers. DisplayPort tops out at 1.4 rather than DisplayPort 2.1. You don’t get the sort of elaborate USB-C docking setup found on productivity-focused displays. None of that bothers me. Give me the fantastic panel at a great price and cut the extras. The humble port selection on the Alienware AW3226Q. Brad Chacos/Foundry Alienware seems to be settling into a compelling strategy with its latest OLED monitors: Spend the money on the screen and ruthlessly attack the price everywhere else. The $350 AW2726DM is the extreme expression of that idea. Strip things down, accept some compromises in brightness and desktop use, and deliver the core OLED gaming experience at a price I would’ve considered ludicrous not long ago. The $699 AW3226Q takes that philosophy upscale. You get a spacious 32-inch 4K Tandem OLED panel with a glossy finish, crisp RGB-stripe text, excellent gaming responsiveness, HDMI 2.1, and a three-year warranty that covers OLED burn-in. Alienware skipped some luxuries, but it didn’t cheap out on the parts of the monitor I actually care about. I’ll take that trade every time. Bottom line: The Alienware AW3226Q is what I wanted OLED monitors to become Cyberpunk and my old writing business pen holder: Only this OLED monitor nails the mix For work and play. Brad Chacos/Foundry A year ago, I couldn’t buy this combination. We’ve had spectacular OLED gaming monitors for years. Fast ones, cheap ones, gorgeous ones. But none I’d happily use for both work and play. The Alienware AW3226Q changes that. During the day, I get a large, sharp 4K desktop with crisp text that doesn’t constantly remind me I’m using an OLED. When work ends, I get the deep blacks, vibrant colors, stunning contrast, and instantaneous response that make OLED gaming so sublime. For $699! There are monitors better suited to specific niches. I’d pick something faster if competitive gaming was my only priority. Someone building an elaborate one-cable laptop workstation may care more about connectivity than I do. But I don’t need the AW3226Q to be the best monitor for every niche. I need it to be excellent at everything I actually do. Fantastically, it is. And for the first time with an OLED, I could put one monitor on my desk and stop thinking about what I’m giving up. This will be my new primary display until Alienware makes me ship it back. No rush, Alienware.

item.title: Nvidia is no longer a PC gaming company. Get used to it
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
I’ve been buying Nvidia graphics cards exclusively for nearly 30 years, and I may well continue—if Nvidia will let me. But even I’ve had to make peace with the fact that Nvidia is no longer in the business of supporting PC gaming. I’m not sure it ever will be again. I was thinking about this while listening to the latest episode of The Full Nerd, in which Adam and his fellow cohosts discuss what it means that Nvidia may soon stop selling the RTX 5090 entirely. The news comes courtesy of a Twitter (sorry, X ) post from a known leaker with a decent track record, so while you should take it with a grain of salt it seems like there’s a strong possibility it will prove true. Welcome to The Full Nerd newsletter—your weekly dose of hardware talk from the enthusiasts at PCWorld. Missed the surprising topics on our YouTube show or the latest news from across the web? You’re in the right place. Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website ! And honestly, it doesn’t seem that surprising when you consider that the RTX 5090 launched with an MSRP of $1,999 yet regularly sold for upwards of $5,000, due in no small part to massive demand from AI-pilled coders and companies looking to take advantage of that sweet, sweet 32GB of DDR7 memory. A casual search of the major retailers this week turned up precisely zero 5090 cards available for purchase, even at that exorbitant price, and I suspect that will remain true for the foreseeable future. It can feel heartbreaking if you’re dedicated to the hardcore DIY PC gaming lifestyle, but you can take solace in the fact that the GeForce RTX 5080, RTX 5070 Ti and RTX 5070 are still widely available and plenty good enough for high-res, high-speed PC gaming. Heck, the same leak that suggests the RTX 5090 is done for also claims that Nvidia will launch a new model of RTX 5080 with 24GB of DDR7 memory, which should offer a noticeable improvement over the current 16GB RTX 5080 cards. But I have to say, the sooner you make peace with the fact that Nvidia is no longer in the business of supporting PC gaming, the better. Don’t get me wrong, Nvidia will continue to make new desktop graphics cards and talk a big game about how it values PC game players first and foremost. But the numbers have shown otherwise for some time, and that’s likely to continue for years to come. After all, the AI-driven explosion of demand for high-end GPUs and silicon helped Nvidia become the first trillion-dollar chip company , and recent financial reports and SEC filings show the company’s revenue from data center products is now 4-5x that of its consumer hardware revenue. That’s presumably part of the reason why the company recently stopped reporting GPU sales as a discrete category entirely, instead lumping all GPU hardware sales (for both commercial and retail customers) into one category on its balance sheet alongside robotics, automotive and telecom products. So please, for your own mental health, I’m begging you: do not give in to Jensen’s sales pitches at the next Nvidia press conference. I believe the company will keep making new graphics cards for the foreseeable future, but only to hold on to its commanding hold of the GPU market and keep up appearances while it milks the AI boom for all its worth. If AI demand collapses the way crypto seemed to crash a few years ago, maybe we’ll see Nvidia take up the mantle of being a PC gaming company once again. But I don’t expect that will happen any time soon, and making peace with that has done wonders for the stress I feel right now as a frustrated fan of PC gaming. It’s helped me realize that I don’t need the latest and greatest hardware to have a blast gaming on my PC, and the same can be true for you. Take this time to play some games in your Steam(ing) pile of shame, get deeper into Linux gaming and explore all the other cool things you can do without an RTX 5090. Because I don’t know that high-end GPUs will be affordable for regular folks like you and me in the next few years, if ever—and I don’t think I’ll be buying an Nvidia GPU any time in the near future. item.title: Explore Reddit like never before with this interactive map
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Just when I think I’ve seen everything Reddit has to offer, some obscure subreddit pops up and proves me wrong. There are seemingly endless numbers of them, so realistically you don’t have enough time to browse your way to the bizarre, underappreciated stuff. But with a site like Map of Reddit , you might be able to find those niche subreddits a bit easier. It’s a free, interactive site that plots more than 116,000 subreddits as dots in one giant galaxy. Each dot represents a community and the closer two dots are together, the more overlap their communities have. The map is built from around 1.5 billion Reddit comments, which makes for a more nuanced and accurate picture of relationships rather than an algorithmic guess at which topics belong together. And you might be surprised at how some of the neighbors are ones you’d never predict—quizzically looking at you Twitter and FBI subreddits. The map is fully interactive so you can click and drag to move around, zoom in, or use the search bar to find a specific subreddit. If you click on a community dot, you’ll get some more information plus links to all of the related subreddits. Personally, I’ve used it to discover a ton of subreddits devoted to hobbies I didn’t even know were a thing. Ever heard of r/BirdsWithArms? Or how about r/HaveWeMet? Reddit is a weird and wonderful place, but sometimes you need a map to find your way. item.title: YouTube Music Introduces AI Labels to Enhance Transparency for Listeners
item.description:
Sources: Ars Technica, Engadget, Latest from Android Central
YouTube Music is rolling out new labels to help users identify tracks created or significantly altered by generative AI, addressing growing concerns about the proliferation of AI-generated music on streaming platforms. The labels, visible on the player page and below track names, will indicate whether a song was fully generated by AI, partially influenced by AI tools, or entirely human-made. This initiative builds on similar efforts by YouTube to label AI-generated content, expanding transparency to music streaming while acknowledging the role of AI in creative processes.
The labels aim to empower listeners by providing clear distinctions between AI-assisted and fully AI-created works. For example, tracks where generative models contributed major components like vocals or composition will be marked, with a tap revealing detailed information about AI involvement. Google emphasized that the labels are not meant to stifle AI innovation but to inform users, as the company stated, "Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music." However, the company also recognized the need for clarity, noting that users "want to know if a song was created with generative AI tools."
The labeling process combines disclosures from music partners with automated detection tools. Partners can specify AI involvement through metadata workflows, categorizing tracks as "Fully Gen AI," "Partly Gen," or "No Gen AI." If creators leave disclosure fields blank, YouTube may still apply labels using its detection systems, which analyze content for signs of AI generation. This dual approach ensures accountability even when creators do not explicitly disclose AI use.
The move comes as AI music production becomes more accessible, prompting streaming services to address listener confusion. Spotify has begun labeling fake artists, while Deezer is implementing filters to reduce AI-generated content. YouTube Music’s labels are also set to extend to its main video platform, further broadening transparency efforts. While the labels do not ban AI music, they reflect a growing industry push to distinguish between human-created and AI-generated content, ensuring users can make informed choices about what they consume.
Critics and users have welcomed the initiative as a step toward standardizing transparency across digital content. As one Android Central contributor noted, "I’d love to see AI labels become the standard for everything I consume online," highlighting the demand for clear disclosure in an era where AI-generated media is increasingly prevalent. By providing context about AI involvement, YouTube Music aims to balance innovation with user trust, ensuring listeners can navigate the evolving landscape of music creation with greater clarity.
